risks.quote: It is important to understand that the information provided by Generative AI may not always be reliable or up to date, for example they have been known to commonly ‘hallucinate’ references which do not exist.

They can synthesise information but are less able to analyse and evaluate the information presented. Weighing up research and presenting a coherent argument that is backed-up with evidence is a very human skill and consequently you cannot rely on Generative AI to do this for you.

Generative AI is only able to generate responses based on the information it has been trained on and the datasets it has access to. Therefore, if the dataset has bias within it, it is likely to be transferred to the information generated.
For most Generative AI tools, by uploading your work you grant the providers the right to use it as they see fit, and this may include sharing it with other people.

When using Generative AI tools, it is important to be aware of copyright laws as they will apply to the content uploaded to the Generative AI interface, the training data used to build the models, and potentially the outputs generated.

One key concern is the environmental impact of digital technologies like GenAI, potentially requiring massive amounts of energy consumption and water, as well as emitting high levels of carbon emissions.

responsibilities.quote: Always double-check and verify information obtained from Generative AI tools.
to ensure you are using the tools effectively and ethically, the following factors should be considered.
If you are using Generative AI tools to collect or process personal data, you need to comply with the DPA.
If you include other people’s personal data into the tools an ethics review might be required.
This includes a commitment to supporting students and PGRs to become ‘AI-literate’.
This guidance will be reviewed and continually updated as generative AI technologies develop.
